coverage: All five chapters and their footnotes in both English editions. Named thinkers, quoted correspondents and religious references; no invented characters for generic moral examples.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: The Athenian philosopher represented in Plato’s dialogues.

entities.name: Protagoras
entities.body: The Greek sophist who debates Socrates in Plato’s dialogue.

entities.name: Plato
entities.body: The Greek philosopher and author of the dialogue featuring Socrates and Protagoras.

entities.name: Jeremy Bentham
entities.body: The British philosopher and reformer associated with the greatest-happiness principle.

entities.name: Immanuel Kant
entities.body: The German philosopher whose account of moral duty Mill discusses.

entities.name: Epicurus
entities.body: The ancient Greek philosopher who made pleasure and freedom from pain central to a good life.

entities.name: Thomas Carlyle
entities.body: The Scottish writer and social critic quoted on the supposed right to happiness.

entities.name: Novalis
entities.body: The German Romantic poet and thinker cited in the discussion of happiness.

entities.name: Jesus of Nazareth
entities.body: The central figure of Christianity, invoked for the Golden Rule and love of others.

entities.name: John Galt
entities.body: The Scottish novelist who wrote Annals of the Parish.

entities.name: The Rev. J. Llewellyn Davis
entities.body: The clergyman who challenges Mill’s example about motives and rescuing a drowning person.

entities.name: Auguste Comte
entities.body: The French philosopher whose system of positive politics Mill discusses.

entities.name: Robert Owen
entities.body: The social reformer cited for his view that circumstances shape a person’s character.

entities.name: Alexander Bain
entities.body: The philosopher and psychologist whose work on the emotions and will Mill cites.

entities.name: Herbert Spencer
entities.body: The philosopher and author of Social Statics who corresponds with Mill about utility.

entities.name: God
entities.body: The divine being discussed in relation to morality, happiness and religious belief.
